lessonTitle: Anaemia: Classification by Red Cell Size, Iron Studies and Pernicious Anaemia

blocks.text: A 34-year-old nurse tells her doctor she is exhausted, gets breathless climbing the stairs on the ward, and has started craving ice. Her periods have been heavy for a year. Her haemoglobin is low and her red cells, seen under the microscope, are small and pale. The size of the red cell is the first clue to why the blood count has fallen.

blocks.title: Anaemia
blocks.text: Anaemia is a reduction in the haemoglobin concentration of the blood below the reference range for age and sex, with a reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. Thresholds vary by laboratory, but the WHO uses about 130 g/L for adult men and 120 g/L for non-pregnant adult women.

blocks.markdown: Anaemia is a sign, not a diagnosis, and always has a cause. Symptoms reflect tissue hypoxia and compensation: fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, pallor and, when severe, angina or heart failure. The most useful first step in finding the cause is the **mean cell volume (MCV)**, the average red cell size, which splits anaemias into **microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic**.

blocks.caption: Mean cell volume. Reference range is roughly 80-100 fL (laboratory dependent).

blocks.title: Calculating MCV
blocks.prompt: A patient has haematocrit 0.27 L/L and a red cell count of 3.0 x 10^12/L. Calculate MCV and classify the anaemia by size.

steps.text: Divide haematocrit by red cell count: 0.27 / 3.0 = 0.090.
Multiply by 1000 to express in femtolitres: 90 fL.
A value of 90 fL lies within 80-100 fL, so the red cells are normal in size.

rows: Iron deficiency (low ferritin); thalassaemia trait (normal ferritin, often a high red cell count); sideroblastic anaemia; some anaemia of chronic disease
Impaired haemoglobin synthesis: cells divide extra times and are small and pale
Acute blood loss; anaemia of chronic disease; chronic kidney disease; haemolysis; marrow failure
Reduced red cell production or loss with normal haemoglobin content per cell
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic); alcohol; hypothyroidism; liver disease; some drugs
Impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation so cells grow large; or membrane lipid excess
blocks.caption: Classification of anaemia by MCV

blocks.markdown:
### Iron studies

Iron deficiency is the commonest cause of anaemia worldwide, from blood loss (menstruation, gastrointestinal bleeding), inadequate intake or poor absorption. Iron is carried in blood by **transferrin**, and stored as **ferritin**. The total capacity of transferrin is the **total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)**, and the percentage of binding sites occupied is the **transferrin saturation**. In **anaemia of chronic disease** (inflammation from infection, autoimmune disease or cancer), cytokines such as IL-6 raise **hepcidin**, which blocks the iron exporter ferroportin. Iron is therefore trapped inside macrophages and enterocytes, and unavailable for erythropoiesis, even though stores are adequate.

blocks.caption: Both in the same units (for example micromol/L).

rows: Normal or raised (acute-phase protein, stores present)
blocks.caption: Distinguishing iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease (ferritin is the single most useful test, but is raised by inflammation)

blocks.title: Interpreting iron studies
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has Hb 102 g/L, MCV 84 fL, serum iron 7 micromol/L, TIBC 40 micromol/L and ferritin 250 microgram/L. Which pattern is this?

steps.text: Transferrin saturation = 7 / 40 x 100 = 17.5%, which is low.
TIBC is not raised and ferritin is high, so iron stores are not depleted. In iron deficiency, ferritin would be low and TIBC high.
Chronic inflammation raises hepcidin and traps iron in macrophages, and the red cells are normocytic or slightly microcytic.

blocks.markdown:
### Pernicious anaemia and vitamin B12 deficiency

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) comes from animal foods. In the stomach it is released from food and binds **intrinsic factor (IF)**, a glycoprotein secreted by gastric **parietal cells**. The B12-IF complex is absorbed in the **terminal ileum**. **Pernicious anaemia** is an autoimmune condition: an autoimmune atrophic gastritis destroys parietal cells, and autoantibodies against parietal cells and against intrinsic factor prevent B12 absorption. Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for DNA synthesis (via methionine synthase, linked to folate metabolism) and for myelin maintenance. Without it, rapidly dividing marrow cells make DNA slowly but RNA and protein normally, so nuclear maturation lags and large **megaloblasts**, hypersegmented neutrophils and a raised MCV result; intramedullary destruction produces mild jaundice and raised lactate dehydrogenase. Demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts causes **subacute combined degeneration** with paraesthesiae, loss of vibration and position sense and spastic weakness.

blocks.title: Do not treat neurological B12 deficiency with folate alone
blocks.text: Folate can improve the anaemia of B12 deficiency but does not prevent, and may let progress, the neurological damage. Always identify which deficiency is present before treating.

points: Anaemia is first classified by MCV: microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia), normocytic (blood loss, chronic disease, kidney disease, haemolysis) and macrocytic (B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism).
Iron deficiency shows low ferritin, low iron, high TIBC and low saturation, whereas anaemia of chronic disease shows normal or high ferritin, low iron, low or normal TIBC because hepcidin traps iron.
Pernicious anaemia is autoimmune loss of parietal cells and intrinsic factor, causing B12 malabsorption in the terminal ileum, megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has Hb 92 g/L and an MCV of 68 fL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: chronic blood loss depletes iron and produces a microcytic anaemia.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: acute haemorrhage causes a normocytic anaemia.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: renal anaemia is normocytic and unrelated to menstrual loss.

questions.explanation: Menstrual blood loss is a leading cause of iron deficiency in women. Lack of iron limits haemoglobin synthesis, so red cells are small and pale, giving a low MCV.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man of Mediterranean descent has a mild microcytic anaemia with MCV 66 fL, a raised red cell count and a normal serum ferritin. Which diagnosis is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: microcytosis with a normal ferritin and a high or normal red cell count suggests reduced globin chain synthesis.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: iron deficiency would show a low ferritin.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia with normocytic cells.

questions.explanation: Reduced globin synthesis in thalassaemia produces small cells, and the marrow compensates by making more of them. Because iron stores are normal, ferritin is normal, which separates it from iron deficiency.

questions.stem: Where is vitamin B12 absorbed, and which cells produce the factor needed for its absorption?

options.text: Terminal ileum; gastric parietal cells produce intrinsic factor
Duodenum; gastric chief cells produce intrinsic factor
Jejunum; pancreatic acinar cells produce intrinsic factor

questions.correctOptionText: Terminal ileum; gastric parietal cells produce intrinsic factor

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the B12-intrinsic factor complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum, and parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: chief cells secrete pepsinogen, and absorption is not in the duodenum.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: pancreatic cells do not secrete intrinsic factor.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: B12 is not absorbed in the colon.

questions.explanation: Intrinsic factor from parietal cells binds B12, and receptors on the terminal ileum take up the complex. Loss of parietal cells in pernicious anaemia therefore abolishes absorption.

questions.stem: A patient has Hb 95 g/L, serum ferritin 6 microgram/L, low serum iron and a high TIBC. What is the most likely cause?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: low ferritin with high TIBC and low iron is characteristic of depleted iron stores.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: anaemia of chronic disease has normal or high ferritin.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: iron overload gives high ferritin and high saturation.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: folate deficiency is macrocytic and does not change iron studies.

questions.explanation: Ferritin reflects stores, so a very low value confirms iron deficiency. The liver makes more transferrin in response, so TIBC rises while serum iron and saturation fall.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has a macrocytic anaemia, tingling feet and impaired vibration sense. Antibodies to intrinsic factor are positive. Which mechanism best explains the neurological findings?

options.text: Demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts from B12 deficiency
Autoimmune destruction of motor neurons by intrinsic factor antibodies

questions.correctOptionText: Demyelination of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts from B12 deficiency

distractorRationale.a: Correct: B12 is needed for myelin maintenance, and deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: iron deposition does not explain these findings.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: intrinsic factor antibodies impair absorption but do not attack neurons.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: folate excess is not the cause.

questions.explanation: Deficiency of B12 impairs myelin maintenance, so dorsal columns (vibration and proprioception) and corticospinal tracts degenerate. This produces sensory loss and, later, spastic weakness.

questions.stem: A patient has a haematocrit of 0.34 L/L and a red cell count of 3.0 x 10^12/L. Calculate the mean cell volume (MCV) in fL.
questions.explanation: MCV = haematocrit / RBC x 1000 = 0.34 / 3.0 x 1000 = 113 fL. This is above the reference range of about 80-100 fL, so the anaemia is macrocytic and a search for B12 or folate deficiency is warranted.

questions.stem: A patient has a serum iron of 5 micromol/L and a total iron-binding capacity of 62.5 micromol/L. Calculate the transferrin saturation as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Transferrin saturation = serum iron / TIBC x 100 = 5 / 62.5 x 100 = 8%. This is markedly low, in keeping with iron deficiency where TIBC is high and the little available iron fills few binding sites.

questions.stem: Classify anaemia by red cell size, giving two causes of each category and the mechanism that explains the cell size.
markingGuide: Microcytic (MCV below about 80 fL): iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, sideroblastic anaemia
Microcytic mechanism: impaired haemoglobin synthesis so cells divide extra times and are small
Normocytic: acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, CKD, haemolysis, marrow failure
Macrocytic (above about 100 fL): B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, liver disease
Macrocytic (megaloblastic) mechanism: impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation so cells enlarge
questions.explanation: MCV reflects the haemoglobin and DNA synthesis balance within the marrow. This single number rapidly narrows the differential and directs further testing.

questions.stem: Explain how iron studies distinguish iron deficiency anaemia from anaemia of chronic disease, including the role of hepcidin.
markingGuide: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation
Anaemia of chronic disease: normal or high ferritin (acute-phase reactant), low iron, low or normal TIBC, low saturation
Hepcidin blocks ferroportin so iron is trapped in macrophages and enterocytes and unavailable to the marrow
Stores are adequate in chronic disease but functional deficiency exists
Ferritin is raised by inflammation so interpretation needs care
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency is a true lack of total body iron, so stores and saturation are low and the liver makes more transferrin. In chronic disease, hepcidin sequesters iron, so supply to the marrow falls despite normal or high stores.

questions.stem: Explain the mechanism of vitamin B12 deficiency in pernicious anaemia and how it produces both the haematological and neurological features.
markingGuide: Autoimmune atrophic gastritis destroys parietal cells; antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor
Loss of intrinsic factor prevents B12 absorption in the terminal ileum
B12 is needed for DNA synthesis; deficiency causes megaloblastic change, macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils
Ineffective erythropoiesis gives pancytopenia in severe cases and mild jaundice
B12 is needed for myelin maintenance; subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts
Folate should not be given alone
questions.explanation: Absence of intrinsic factor prevents B12 absorption despite adequate diet. Impaired DNA synthesis slows nuclear maturation of marrow cells, while impaired myelin maintenance damages the spinal cord.
